data.title: Trenčín – a Great Moravian hillfort beneath the castle rock
data.excerpt: Trenčín Castle rises on a steep limestone crag above the town, but the history of the site did not begin with the Kingdom of Hungary. In the time of Great Moravia a hillfort with a triangular ground plan stood here, and a masonry rotunda was built on its acropolis — one of the few Great Moravian stone buildings known from the territory of present-day Slovakia. The remains of its rampart are still legible in the Čerešňový sad locality.
data.metaTitle: Trenčín – a Great Moravian hillfort under the castle rock
data.metaDescription: The castle rock above the Váh at Trenčín was occupied long before Hungary. A major Great Moravian hillfort with a rotunda stood here.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: A steep limestone crag directly above the town of Trenčín, the landmark of the Middle Váh region

keyFacts.label: Hillfort and acropolis
keyFacts.value: Originally a triangular ground plan; one corner extended into the area of the later medieval castle (the acropolis)

keyFacts.label: The Great Moravian rotunda
keyFacts.value: A circular nave 750 cm in diameter, later rebuilt into a tetraconch with 4 band-like conches (315 – 380 cm wide)

keyFacts.label: Parallels for the rotunda
keyFacts.value: Dimensions and building technique identical with the rotundas at Ducové, Staré Mesto and Levý Hradec — confirming a Great Moravian origin

keyFacts.label: Neighbouring hillforts
keyFacts.value: Skalka (a small church with a semicircular apse), Čertova skala (Trenčianska Teplá) and Hradište — probably refuges or watch posts

keyFacts.label: The earliest counts of Trenčín
keyFacts.value: Bogomel (12th c.), Noska and Přemysl — Slavic names, with no marked presence of ethnic Hungarians

keyFacts.label: Continuity of the centre
keyFacts.value: Comparable with Bratislava, Devín, Zvolen and Bojná — a Great Moravian administrative centre surviving into the Kingdom of Hungary

timeline.description: A fortified settlement and trading centre with a Celtic population maintaining relations with the Celts of the Middle Danube (the find of a gold Athena Alknis coin and of Biatec tetradrachms).

timeline.title: A Roman inscription on the castle rock
timeline.description: A Latin inscription attests to the victory of the Roman army (the Second Auxiliary Legion) over Germanic tribes at Laugaricio during the reign of Marcus Aurelius.

timeline.title: Construction of the Great Moravian hillfort
timeline.description: A triangular ground plan with a box-rampart construction similar to that of the hillfort at Pobedim; the entrance from the south, narrowing towards the acropolis.

timeline.title: Building of the Great Moravian rotunda
timeline.description: A simple rotunda with an internal apse (nave diameter 750 cm) on the acropolis — dimensions and building technique typical of Ducové, Staré Mesto and Levý Hradec.

timeline.title: The tetraconch rebuilding of the rotunda
timeline.description: New elements set out using the Hungarian royal foot, paralleled by the tetraconch of SS Peter and Paul at Székesfehérvár — possibly to be linked with the activities of Stephen I.

timeline.title: Indirect evidence for the province of Trenčín
timeline.description: The charter on the foundation of the bishopric of Prague mentions the province of Váh, with its centre probably at Trenčín.

timeline.title: The first written report of the castle
timeline.description: The chronicle of Cosmas confirms the existence of the castle; the later Bohemian king Bretislav II was reportedly received and lodged here.

timeline.title: The Zobor charters
timeline.description: Trenčín is mentioned as civitas Treinchen — a town.

timeline.title: The hillfort ceases to fulfil its function
timeline.description: Building activity continued only on the acropolis; Trenčín remained the seat of a county until the early modern period.

timeline.title: The rampart confirmed as functional in the 12th century

mediaTexts.caption: A legend attaches to the castle well, about the love of the Turkish nobleman Omar for the beautiful Fatima, a captive of Štefan Zápoľský, the lord of Trenčín Castle. In order to set Fatima free, Omar promised to dig a well in the hard rock of Trenčín Castle. For three years he dug with his companions, until the rock really did yield water, but only a few of the diggers survived. Omar handed the first cup of water to Zápoľský with the words: "You have water, Zápoľský, but you have no heart". When Omar was taking the freed Fatima away from the castle on horseback, her veil caught on a briar bush. On that spot stands, to this day, the oldest inn in Trenčín, called "Fatima", or in earlier times also "Závoj" (The Veil).

children.text: The majestic Trenčín Castle, one of the most important and most beautiful castles in Slovakia, rises on a steep limestone crag directly above the town of Trenčín. It is a characteristic landmark not only of Trenčín but of the whole Middle Váh region. The castle is inseparably linked with one of the best-known figures of Slovak (Hungarian) history — Matúš Čák. The first written report confirming the existence of the castle, in 1091, is found in the chronicle of Cosmas. The town, civitas Treinchen, is recorded in 1111. Its history, however, did not begin only with the emergence of the Kingdom of Hungary; it is far older.

The strategic position of the castle hill is self-evident, and for that reason almost all the more important prehistoric cultures left traces of occupation here. The earliest archaeological finds attest to a human presence in Trenčín and its surroundings as early as 200,000 years ago in prehistory. Ancient occupation is represented by a settlement site of the
Maďarovce culture
of the 2nd millennium BC, of the Late Bronze Age, on the castle rock, and by the remains of a settlement of the
Lusatian culture

of the Final Bronze Age, from the turn of the 2nd and 1st millennia BC, on the castle rock and in the adjoining part of Brezina. At the same site archaeological excavation also revealed the remains of occupation by the people of the
Púchov culture
of the Iron Age. In the 2nd and 1st centuries a fortified settlement and trading centre of the late La Tène period existed here, whose
Celtic population

maintained trading relations with the Celts of the Middle Danube, as is shown by the find of a gold Celtic coin of the Athena Alknis type and two silver tetradrachms of the Biatec type of the Bratislava Boii.
Already in the centuries before the arrival of the Celts, one of the branches of the famous
Amber Road
ran through the territory of Trenčín

, through the Vlára Pass and on along the basin of the Morava; along it Etruscan, Greek and later Roman merchants travelled from the Mediterranean region to the Baltic. From the north they brought precious amber, for which they paid with luxury products of classical craftsmen and with wine.

children.text: At
Laugaricio
, probably present-day Trenčín, a battle between Germanic tribes and Roman legionaries of the Second Auxiliary Legion took place in the 2nd century during the reign of
Marcus Aurelius

. We learn of the victory of the Roman army from a Latin inscription on the castle rock dated 179. It was precisely the knowledge of the presence of Roman troops that prompted the excavation at the castle in the Čerešňový sad locality in the 1950s. It was thought that the ramparts visible in the terrain might be the remains of a Roman camp, which was not confirmed; prehistoric and early medieval occupation was, however, identified.
The hillfort and the castle acropolis
The hillfort
in the time of Great Moravia

originally had a triangular ground plan, and one of its corners extended into the area where the medieval castle was later built (the castle acropolis). On the basis of the configuration of the terrain it is likely that the entrance to the hillfort was from the south and that the hillfort narrowed towards the north (the acropolis). The construction of the rampart was probably
of box type, and the walls
were deliberately strengthened by firing. The Trenčín rampart at Čerešňový sad has many similarities with the rampart of the hillfort at Pobedim, dated to the first third of the 9th century.

The area of the hillfort was systematically lowered in the early modern period, so that the occupation layers were lost over roughly three quarters of the ground plan of the hillfort; the remains of the rampart defences are nevertheless still legible in the terrain, and excavation in the 1980s even confirmed that they were still functional in the 12th century. The castle acropolis was evidently part of the hillfort, but it may also have been separated from it by a ditch, which is only very difficult to verify by field excavation. In the 15th–16th centuries, in connection with advances in the development of firearms, substantial changes were made to the terrain here, and later a star-shaped fortification was built. The access route to the acropolis either ran along the narrow neck (or possibly over a bridge above an artificially cut ditch), or there may have been a palisade wall here separating the acropolis from the wider “bailey” — the hillfort at Čerešňový sad. Among the finds from the area of the lower castle dating from the time of Great Moravia, the most notable are vessels, bucket hoops, a spindle whorl, a
gombík
(a spherical hollow metal button with a loop), a quern and many sherds.
The Great Moravian rotunda

Excavation on the acropolis in the 1970s uncovered a sacral building with a centralised plan – a rotunda. The structure consists of a circular nave 750 cm in diameter, which was divided by four band-like blocks into a tetraconch. The width of the conches ranged between 315 and 380 cm, and the crown masonry of the conches was 65–75 cm thick. In the reveals of the conches, columns made up of worked stone drums 35–50 cm in diameter were set on square plinths.

The building was respected by graves, which contained an S-shaped temple ring and coins allowing the conclusion that the rotunda was already standing in the 11th century. Finds from the 9th century occurred in a 20 cm layer of black soil which, among other things, also contained an iron bearded axe. Another 9th-century layer, about 60 cm thick, lay beneath the former access road to the castle near the rotunda. Archaeologists and historians held differing views on the dating of the rotunda. T. Nešporová, V. Jankovič, M. Slivka and Z. Ševčíková assumed that the building originated in the 9th century and placed the tetraconch rebuilding in the 11th century. Martin Vančo, in his book Stredoveké rotundy na Slovensku 9. – 13. storočie (Medieval Rotundas in Slovakia, 9th–13th Centuries), published in 2000, states that the masonry of the rotunda contains elements demonstrating different building phases of the structure. The original building can be described as a simple rotunda with an internal apse. The first phase has a nave diameter of 750 cm, a semicircular apse 350 cm wide and masonry 65–75 cm thick. The dimensions of the rotunda, the use of the Roman foot as the building measure and the building technique are typical of several Great Moravian rotundas — Ducové, Staré Mesto and Levý Hradec — and on this basis the hypotheses about the Great Moravian origin of the rotunda can be confirmed. In the second building phase the new architectural elements were set out on the basis of the Hungarian royal foot, used for example in the construction of the tetraconch of SS Peter and Paul at Székesfehérvár at the turn of the 10th/11th century. According to this parallel, it would be possible to link this rebuilding of the rotunda with the activities of Stephen I in building the Hungarian state in the first third of the 11th century. The relationship between the rotunda and the older tower identified within the present brick tower will remain a subject of scholarly discussion. It can therefore be concluded that

the rotunda at Trenčín Castle was built while Great Moravia still existed, and it must therefore be counted among the small number of masonry Great Moravian buildings from the territory of present-day Slovakia.

children.text: The prevailing view is that in the case of Trenčín we can speak of an important early feudal seat. The rotunda in this layout is understood as a certain precursor of the castle chapel. In the case of the Trenčín rotunda this is all the more evident because the rotunda really did fulfil such a function until the beginning of the 15th century. The stone tower at Trenčín evidently served both a residential and a defensive function. For the situation in the 11th–12th centuries the existence of a palace is also very likely, at first probably of timber and later of masonry. At some point in the 12th/13th century the hillfort as a whole gradually ceased to fulfil its function, and building activity continued only in the area of the acropolis. Because Trenčín Castle was the seat of a county until the early modern period, in the stage of development up to the 12th century we can speak of a central hillfort, and its function as an administrative centre for a wider region is very likely. Trenčín already fulfilled the function of a central hillfort in the Great Moravian period.
The importance of Trenčín in the Early Middle Ages

children.text: In the wider area around Trenčín we find traces of relatively dense occupation in the 9th–11th centuries. In most cases the archaeological finds were come upon by chance, without any subsequent systematic excavation. This is evidently an
early medieval settlement agglomeration

, which we can understand as the economic hinterland of the centre on the castle rock. The Trenčín hillfort was the most important in the region in the 9th–12th centuries, but not the only one; another lay at Skalka, where a small church with a semicircular apse was identified. In the cadastral area of the village of Trenčianska Teplá there is a hillfort in the locality known as Čertova skala. The locality called Hradište lies where the road from the Hrozenkov pass opens into the Váh valley. In the case of these hillforts their role as refuges, or possibly as watch posts, can be considered. When Trenčín and its surroundings were definitively incorporated into the Kingdom of Hungary, the Hungarian rulers merely respected the earlier development; that is, this territory was perceived as an already formed region with its administrative centre at Trenčín Castle. The Hungarian rulers were likewise not the immediate organisers of Christianisation in this region, which testifies to an older genesis of Christianity among the local population.
In the Middle Ages Trenčín was the seat of an administrative unit called a župa
, that is a county (Latin comitatus), headed by a count. From the second half of the 12th century written sources also record some
names of the earliest counts of Trenčín
. In the 12th century a certain
Bogomel, son of Soběslav
, is mentioned as comes. The Slavic personal names of other defenders and servants of the castle,
Noska and Přemysl
(iobbagiones castri de Trenchin), also mean that we need not assume any marked presence of members of the Hungarian ethnic group among the local population. In terms of nationality, then, the
counts of Trenčín
in the early period evidently
were not ethnic Hungarians
, although naturally, given the office they held, they belonged to the “natio Hungarica”, while their nationality was Slovak.

children.text: On the basis of present knowledge Trenčín can be regarded as an example of the
continuity
of a strategically
important Great Moravian seat
, with its own economic hinterland, right
into the period of the Kingdom of Hungary

. Its importance can be compared, for example, with Bratislava, Devín, Zvolen, Bojná and other centres. The existence of Trenčín is recorded in written sources that tell of the historical situation of the 11th century. These are above all the already mentioned
chronicle of Cosmas
(1119 – 1125), where Trenčín is mentioned as
Trencinopolis
, and the
Illuminated Chronicle of Vienna

. In 1091 the later Bohemian king Bretislav II (1092 – 1100) was reportedly welcomed at Trenčín Castle and lodged there with his leading supporters. Indirect testimony to the existence of Trenčín at the beginning of the 11th century is also provided by the
legend of Maurus
, written before 1074. From the 12th century directly preserved charter sources are known, above all the
Zobor charters

dated to 1111 and 1113. Trenčín is mentioned there as a civitas (et in civitate Treinchen), that is, as a town. Historians regard as further indirect evidence for the existence of a province at Trenčín the charter on the
foundation of the bishopric of Prague

of 29 April 1086, which among other things mentions the province of Váh; it is assumed that this refers to the territory in the area of the middle course of the Váh, with its centre at Trenčín. 
 
 The fine legend of the well of love is inseparably linked with the existence of Trenčín Castle.

blocks.text: How did the name Laugaricio come about?

children.text: A bonus for those who have read the article to the end:

In the 2nd century, when the foot of the Roman tyrant furtively crossed the Danube and began to poke its insatiable nose into Slovak affairs, our land was of course inhabited by none other than the Old Slovaks. Even at that time they had one of their great cities on the site of Trenčín, which was already called that back then (it can certainly be found on a certain unnamed map of the 2nd century); and the city was known, among other things, for producing the finest and most fashionable garments in the whole Great Moravian Empire – ever since then Trenčín has been called the City of Fashion. So it is no wonder that those effeminate Roman homosexuals took it into their heads to seize precisely this great Slovak city, with which they of course pursued a single aim – to take over the most lucrative markets of the clothing industry. They therefore decided to take Trenčín by storm and directed their entire military machine towards that goal. Few people know that even at that time Trenčín extended over both banks of the river Váh, or, as those Roman scoundrels abusively called it, Vagus Fluvius. The two parts of the great city were joined by a wooden footbridge that led from one bank of the river to the other. The main attack of the Roman army was of course aimed at the castle hill and the settlement below it.

children.text: Our ancestors – the Old Slovaks – waged a heroic and relentless struggle against the Roman aggressors, but because of the considerable numerical superiority and better supply of the Roman army this struggle was doomed to failure. When our ancestors saw that they could no longer repel the Roman onslaught and that the castle and the settlement below it would inevitably fall, they decided to carry out plan B – a retreat across the wooden footbridge to the other side of the Váh, where they assumed the Roman army would not get. When the Romans saw this brilliant military manoeuvre of our ancestors, they immediately set off onto that strategically important footbridge in order to reach the other bank by means of it. But the brilliant tactical brain of our ancestors had reckoned with this treacherous behaviour of the Romans, and at the moment when the footbridge was full of Roman soldiers our ancestors released the footbridge from the banks in a previously devised manner and tipped it, together with part of the Roman army, straight into the raging waves of the Váh. That decided the battle – the Romans knew that although they had taken the castle hill, they had not got the Old Slovaks, nor all their property, which they had carried over to the other bank beforehand. And at the very moment when the footbridge crashed into the Váh with a mighty roar, our ancestors on the other bank called out loudly, as befits proper men of the Váh region:
Lávka v rici Ó, Lávka v rici Ó

[“the footbridge is up the arse, oh” – in Slovak it sounds like Laugaricio]. And since those Roman boors did not understand our language, they thought the people were shouting the name of the town. And from then on the Romans believed that Trenčín was called
Laugarício
, which they then immortalised in that notorious inscription on the Trenčín rock, in celebration of their insignificant and partial victory over the Old Slovaks.
